after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Find the shortest distance between the point $P(4,-2,7)$ and the plane $Π$ with equation $r\cdot ⟨-3,2,3⟩=27.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a point on the plane. If $r=⟨x,y,z⟩,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨-3,2,3⟩ & =27 \\ -3x+2y+3z & =27 \\ 3z & =27+3x-2y \\ z & =9+x-\frac{2}{3}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $x=6$ and $y=3,$ we get 

$$
z=9+6-\frac{2}{3}(3)=13.
$$

So, the point $Q(6,3,13)$ lies on the plane. 

Now, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨6,3,13⟩-⟨4,-2,7⟩ \\  & =⟨2,5,6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the equation of a plane, we get a normal vector $n=⟨-3,2,3⟩.$

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|2\cdot (-3)+5\cdot 2+6\cdot 3|}{\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{3}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|-6+10+18|}{\sqrt{9+4+9}} \\  & =\frac{|22|}{\sqrt{22}} \\  & =\sqrt{22}\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: Find the shortest distance between the point $P(2,1,3)$ and the plane $Π$ with equation $3x-6y-6z=-15.$
after.worked_solution:
Let's start by picking a point on the plane. To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for $x$ and $y$ into the equation and solve for $z.$ Let's choose $x=1$ and $y=-1$ (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for $z,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-6y-6z & =-15 \\ 3(1)-6(-1)-6z & =-15 \\ -6z & =-24 \\ z & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(1,-1,4)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨1,-1,4⟩-⟨2,1,3⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,-2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨3,-6,-6⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|(-1)\cdot 3+(-2)\cdot (-6)+1\cdot (-6)|}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+(-6)^{2}+(-6)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|-3+12-6|}{\sqrt{9+36+36}} \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{81}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
Let's start by picking a point on the plane. To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for $x$ and $y$ into the equation and solve for $z.$ Let's choose $x=1$ and $y=-1$ (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for $z,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-6y-6z & =-15 \\ 3(1)-6(-1)-6z & =-15 \\ -6z & =-24 \\ z & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(1,-1,4)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨1,-1,4⟩-⟨2,1,3⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,-2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨3,-6,-6⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|(-1)\cdot 3+(-2)\cdot (-6)+1\cdot (-6)|}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+(-6)^{2}+(-6)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|-3+12-6|}{\sqrt{9+36+36}} \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{81}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$
